result: Natural antibody repertoire is essential for elimination of neoantigen-expressing cells. WT and Aicda−/− mice (hyper-IgM) rejected 129/BL6 neoantigen-expressing cells, while IgHEL mice (hypo-IgM, lacking antibody repertoire) failed to reject these cells. Reconstitution with naive WT serum restored rejection capacity in IgHEL mice.
evaluation: Claims C25, C26, C62, and C63 provide converging experimental evidence from the 129/BL6 neoantigen model showing that NAb repertoire is required for rejection. The data demonstrate both loss-of-function (IgHEL mice fail to reject) and rescue (serum reconstitution restores rejection), providing strong support for the conclusion (C6).

result: IgHEL mice retain normal adaptive immune function when provided with exogenous licensing signals. When immunized with OVA and poly I:C (TLR3 ligand), IgHEL mice mounted CTL responses similar to WT mice against OVA-expressing cells.
evaluation: Claims C27 and C28 demonstrate that IgHEL mice have intact DC migration and can mount normal CTL responses when DCs are licensed by PAMPs (poly I:C), establishing that the defect in tumor immunity is specifically due to lack of NAbs rather than general immune dysfunction. This control experiment is well-designed and supports the specificity of the NAb requirement.

result: B cell-deficient mouse models show differential tumor susceptibility. muMT mice displayed similar tumor burden to WT mice, while IgHEL and CD19creDTA mice showed 3-5 fold increased tumor burden in both B16F10 melanoma and urethane-induced lung cancer models.
evaluation: Claims C3-C5, C32-C33 are supported by experimental data in Figures 1D-E showing consistent results across multiple B cell-deficient models and tumor types. The discrepancy between muMT and other B cell-deficient models is reproducible and forms the basis for investigating compensatory mechanisms. Sample sizes appear adequate (4-5 mice per group) with statistical significance reported.

result: muMT mice exhibit significantly increased plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs) compared to WT mice. pDCs were identified by co-expression of Ly6C/Ly6D or B220/SiglecH markers, with all B220+ cells in muMT mice being SiglecH+. pDCs showed unique clustering in the 'absentee B cell zone' of lymph nodes in muMT mice, independent of CXCR5 expression.
evaluation: Claims C34-C41 are well-supported by flow cytometry (Figure 2A) and immunohistochemistry data (Figure 2B). Multiple markers were used to identify pDCs, and the distinction from residual B cells is clearly demonstrated. The anatomical localization data adds important context. Statistical significance is shown for pDC frequency differences.

result: pDCs in muMT mice infiltrate tumors and produce IFN-α, providing compensatory anti-tumor immunity. Tumor-bearing muMT mice had significantly more pDCs in the tumor microenvironment expressing high levels of IFN-α. Depleting pDCs in muMT mice resulted in 3-fold increased tumor burden compared to non-depleted muMT and WT mice.
evaluation: Claims C46-C48 and C9 are supported by IHC quantification (Figure 3A) and pDC depletion experiments (Figure 3B). The depletion strategy is detailed in Figure 3—figure supplement 2, showing 63-83% depletion efficiency. The causal relationship between pDC presence and tumor control is demonstrated through the depletion experiment with appropriate controls.

result: Reconstitution of NAbs in pDC-depleted muMT mice partially restores anti-tumor immunity. Administration of naive WT serum to tumor-bearing pDC-depleted muMT mice significantly reduced tumor growth compared to pDC-depletion alone.
evaluation: Claim C49 is supported by experimental data in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 3, demonstrating that NAbs can provide anti-tumor immunity even when the compensatory pDC mechanism is removed. This is a critical experiment linking the two major findings of the paper.

result: muMT mice show increased NK cell infiltration in tumors dependent on pDCs. Tumor-bearing muMT mice had significantly more NK cells in the tumor microenvironment than WT mice, and NK cell frequency was diminished after pDC depletion.
evaluation: Claims C53, C54, and C8 are supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 3C) showing both increased NK cells in muMT tumors and their dependence on pDCs. The data establish a mechanistic link between pDCs and NK cell recruitment.

result: The pDC-IFN-α-NK cell axis constitutes the primary compensatory anti-tumor mechanism in muMT mice. Neutralizing IFN-α increased tumor burden in muMT but not WT mice. NK cell depletion caused 5-fold increased tumor burden in muMT mice compared to WT mice, suggesting this axis is the main anti-tumor mechanism in muMT mice while WT mice have additional mechanisms.
evaluation: Claims C55-C59 are supported by IFN-α neutralization (Figure 3D) and NK cell depletion experiments (Figure 3E). The differential effects in muMT vs WT mice support the compensatory mechanism hypothesis. The experiments are well-controlled and the conclusions logically follow from the data. Statistical significance is demonstrated.

result: Natural antibodies from WT and Aicda mice bind to B16F10 melanoma cells, while serum from IgHEL, Rag2−/−, and muMT mice shows no binding. Western blot and immunohistochemistry demonstrated IgM binding to B16F10 cells only with serum containing diverse antibody repertoires.
evaluation: Claims C60-C61 are supported by Western blot (Figure 4A-B) and IHC data (Figure 4C) showing differential IgM binding patterns. The use of multiple B cell-deficient models as negative controls strengthens the conclusion that a diverse NAb repertoire is required for tumor cell recognition.

result: NAb reconstitution partially reduces tumor burden in IgHEL mice. In the B16F10 melanoma model, IgHEL mice given naive WT serum showed significantly reduced tumor burden compared to untreated IgHEL mice, though still higher than WT mice.
evaluation: Claim C64 is supported by experimental data in Figure 4E showing partial rescue of the tumor phenotype. The incomplete rescue may reflect timing, dose, or the need for continuous NAb presence, which is appropriately acknowledged by the authors.

result: B cells secreting NAbs are critical for detection and elimination of nascent cancer cells through innate immune mechanisms. A complete NAb repertoire is required to identify altered 'self' and initiate elimination of neoantigen-expressing cells. NAbs function as early defense against precancerous cells, initiating both innate and adaptive immune responses.
evaluation: Claims C65, C79, C10, C80-C82 represent the major conclusions synthesized from all experimental data. The conclusions are well-supported by converging evidence from multiple mouse models, tumor types, depletion/reconstitution experiments, and mechanistic studies. The characterization of NAbs as 'keys' that start immune responses is supported but somewhat metaphorical.

result: Proposed mechanism: NAbs tag nascent precancerous cells for clearance through complement activation, engulfment by C1q-secreting interstitial macrophages, surveying monocytes, and NK cell antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity.
evaluation: Claims C66-C67 represent a speculative mechanistic model explicitly stated as 'requiring further investigation.' While consistent with the data and supported by citations to prior work on macrophages and monocytes, the specific mechanistic steps have not been directly tested in this manuscript. This is appropriately presented as a hypothesis for future work.

result: Historical reliance on muMT mice delayed discovery of B cell roles in anti-tumor immunity. Despite known immune abnormalities in muMT mice (reduced T cells, absent follicular DCs, poor lymphatic development), these mice were used to define B cell roles in anti-tumor immunity for decades. Other B cell-deficient models and antibody depletion studies showed contradictory results suggesting B cells mediate early anti-tumor immunity.
evaluation: Claims C68-C69 and C22-C24 are supported by citations to prior literature (Supplementary file 1) and the authors' own comparative data. The critique of field practices is justified by the demonstrated compensatory mechanism in muMT mice. However, the claim about 'delaying discovery' (C69) is somewhat subjective, though reasonable given the evidence.

result: Proposed explanation for muMT compensatory mechanism: pDCs and B cells share a common lymphoid progenitor, and the genetic defect preventing B cell differentiation may permit increased pDC differentiation. The resulting abundance of pDCs enables sufficient migration into tumors to mount anti-tumor responses.
evaluation: Claims C70-C73 mix established knowledge (C70, C72 supported by citations) with speculation (C71, C73). While the shared progenitor is documented and the increased pDC numbers are demonstrated, the mechanistic explanation for why the muMT mutation leads to increased pDCs is speculative. The authors appropriately present this as a hypothesis.

result: NAbs contribute to both innate and adaptive anti-tumor immunity, while DC1 mainly contributes to adaptive immunity. IgHEL mice (deficient in both NAb-mediated innate and DC1-dependent adaptive responses) develop more tumors than DC1-deficient mice (deficient only in adaptive immunity).
evaluation: Claims C74-C77 are supported by citation to prior work (Atif et al., 2018) and logical inference from comparative tumor burdens. The reasoning that dual deficiency causes greater tumor burden than single deficiency is sound, though claim C77 is somewhat circular in its logic.

result: Site of tumor development may affect NAb requirement. B16F10 injections in skin may generate more DAMPs, potentially bypassing the need for NAbs to mount anti-tumor immunity.
evaluation: Claim C78 is explicitly speculative ('may') and represents an alternative hypothesis to explain potential context-dependent variation in results. This is appropriately presented as speculation without supporting data in the manuscript.

result: Characterization of B cell-deficient mouse models used in the study. muMT mice lack CD19+ B cells; IgHEL mice have >90% of B cells specific for hen egg lysozyme (hypo-IgM); CD19creDTA mice have 70-90% fewer B cells due to B1 cell loss; Aicda mice have only IgM (hyper-IgM); 129 strain has allelic variations outside MHC locus relative to C57BL/6.
evaluation: Claims C29-C31, C83-C85 describe established characteristics of the mouse models used, supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 1C) and citations to original papers describing these strains. These are well-established facts necessary for interpreting the experimental results.

result: Cell line quality control: B16F10 melanoma and LLC1 tumor cells were confirmed free of mycoplasma contamination and authenticated through STR DNA profiling.
evaluation: Claim C86 describes standard quality control procedures that are stated in the methods. While important for reproducibility, no data is shown, but this is standard practice for such quality control statements.

result: Background knowledge claims about cancer immunoediting and the current state of the field. Myeloid, T, and NK cells are key players in elimination phase; DCs require licensing by DAMPs/PAMPs; newly transformed cells lack PAMPs; NAbs are currently thought to have no role in cancer surveillance.
evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C11-C15, and C21 represent background knowledge and field context supported by appropriate citations. These establish the rationale for the study. Claim C2 about NAbs being 'overlooked' is supported by the subsequent literature discussion (C21-C24).

result: Prior work on neoantigen models: Male cells are rejected in syngeneic female mice due to H-Y antigens; MHC-matched 129Sv cells are rejected in C57BL/6 mice due to allelic variations outside MHC; these cells have normal MHC-I and no PAMPs; NAbs are required for elimination through a chain-link reaction involving monocytes, CD11c+Irf4-dependent cells, CD4 T cells, and DC1.
evaluation: Claims C16-C20 describe prior published work (primarily Atif et al., 2018) that provides the foundation for the current study. These are appropriately cited and establish the precedent for investigating NAb roles in cancer immunity.

result: Background on pDC biology: pDCs are lymphoid in origin, potent anti-viral and anti-tumor cells that can promote or suppress tumors depending on activation state. pDCs produce type I IFNs (especially IFN-α) in larger quantities than other cell types. In WT mice, pDCs recruit and activate NK cells in tumors, and type I IFN signaling is associated with NK cell-mediated tumor surveillance.
evaluation: Claims C35, C42-C45, C50-C52 represent established knowledge about pDC biology supported by appropriate citations. This background is necessary for interpreting the compensatory mechanism findings and is accurately presented.
